Area.evidence_source: The type of stress Ryan was reported as suffering was suggested by Burns (1980) and Pacht (1984) to be symptomatic of neurotic perfectionism (Hamacheck, 1978) where individuals are driven by relentless standards to the point of agony. An inability to enjoy the fruits of his accomplishment, according to Hamacheck (1978), is also characteristic of neurotic or maladaptive perfectionism and seemed to be shared experiences among the case studies. Not only is perfection an undesirable goal, from this point of view, it is a debilitating one as well. The drive for perfection maintains people in psychological turmoil precisely because that perfection is nonexistent. An intense need to avoid failure was argued by Blatt (1995) to force the neurotically perfectionistic individual into an endless cycle of self-defeating over-striving in which each task becomes another threatening challenge, as seemed to be happening to Dan in particular. Blatt (1995) also argued that the inability to enjoy accomplishments is characteristic of neurotic perfectionism and can result in increased susceptibility to depression and suicide. Burns (1980) argued that when students (with entrenched perfectionistic thinking patterns) begin to realize that their performance will place them somewhere in the middle of the pack, they react with frustration, anger, depression, and panic. This seemed applicable to the case of Sam. Burns (1980) further suggested that as the gap between expectation and actual performance widens, students begin to experience stress and an aversion to learning. This may also be accompanied by painful mood swings and loss of self-esteem, which happened for Sam. The portrait of Sam that emerged from his ex-girlfriend is consistent with Burns' (1980) characterization of perfectionistic individuals as "compulsives" who are especially given to troubled relationships and mood disorders. This type of cognitive distortion, according to Burns (1980), brings fear of mistakes and overreaction. It also leads to overgeneralizations (systems of cognitive distortion common among perfectionists), where they jump to the conclusion that a negative event will be repeated endlessly and predict negative future outcomes (hence his perception that he had a social problem and also his fear of appearing foolish or inadequate among his peers). Blatt (1995) accounts for the destructiveness of this type of personality style by arguing that intense perfectionism can result in a marked vulnerability to experiences of failure and criticism, and an increased susceptibility to ensuing depression and suicide, as seemed to be happening to the young men described here. Because their previous experiences have left them psychologically unprepared for an "average" role, they are prone to perceive themselves, unrealistically, as second rate losers. Their self-respect plummets, and they experience a strong desire to withdraw from painful circumstances. The disturbance can become so intense that they may contemplate and even attempt suicide.
